entities.name: All-India Muslim League founded at Dhaka
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The All-India Muslim League, founded at Dhaka (then Dacca, in British India's Bengal province) on December 30, 1906 — was the political organization that ultimately achieved the creation of Pakistan in 1947, representing the political consciousness of South Asia's Muslim minority within the British Indian Empire and eventually adopting Mohammad Ali Jinnah's 'Two-Nation Theory' that Muslims and Hindus were separate nations requiring separate states.

The 1906 Dhaka founding occurred when Muslim leaders gathered for the All-India Muhammadan Educational Conference at the invitation of the Nawab of Dhaka, Khwaja Salimullah, who was the primary organizer. The founding context was the 1905 Partition of Bengal (later reversed in 1911) and Muslim leaders' concerns about Hindu-dominated Indian National Congress's political power in a future self-governing India. The league initially sought constitutional protections for Muslims within a unified India rather than separation.

The transformation from a Muslim political organization seeking constitutional protections to a independence movement demanding Pakistan is one of the most dramatic political evolutions in modern history: under Muhammad Ali Jinnah's leadership (from 1913, increasingly dominant after 1934), the League shifted from supporting Congress's Indian nationalism to the 1940 Lahore Resolution demanding a separate Muslim state. The 1947 Partition of India — creating Pakistan and resulting in one of history's largest forced migrations (approximately 10-20 million people displaced, and 200,000-2,000,000 killed in communal violence) — was the League's ultimate legacy.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The All-India Muslim League founded at Dhaka — which evolved from Muslim constitutional advocacy to achieving the creation of Pakistan in 1947, one of the 20th century's most significant and violent political transformations — is one of modern history's most consequential political organizations.
